U.S. businesses using contingency-fee or ghost-preparer promoters remain solely liable for disallowed credits, 20% accuracy-related penalties, and examinations reaching back seven or more years, so claims need contemporaneous, project-level substantiation.
Executive Regulatory Overview: The IRS Dirty Dozen and IRC Section 41 Enforcement

The Internal Revenue Service (IRS) consistently designates improper claims for the Research and Experimentation (R&E) tax credit under Internal Revenue Code (IRC) § 41 as a primary enforcement priority, having formally placed abusive research credit schemes on its annual "Dirty Dozen" list of tax scams under "Excessive Claims for Business Credits" from 2016 through 2019 (IR-2016-22, IR-2016-29, IR-2017-27, IR-2017-37, IR-2018-66, and IR-2019-49) and again in 2021 (IR-2021-144), while reinforcing enforcement against the underlying promoter tactics in its 2025 Dirty Dozen compliance warnings (IR-2025-26, issued February 27, 2025). While the 2025 Dirty Dozen release did not contain a standalone R&D credit heading, it explicitly targeted the operational mechanisms utilized by predatory credit promoters—specifically unscrupulous "ghost tax preparers" who refuse to sign returns or omit their Preparer Tax Identification Numbers (PTINs), percentage-of-refund fee arrangements, and misleading tax credit or debt-resolution "mills". The agency characterizes aggressive, unsubstantiated research credit promotions as among the most severe compliance threats confronting businesses because fraudulent or negligent advisory operations expose claimants to multi-year examination liabilities, full credit disallowance, statutory 20% accuracy-related penalties, and substantial legal defense expenditures. Within the federal tax controversy landscape, predatory advisory firms that prioritize volume-driven credit inflation over statutory substantiation are designated as "R&D tax credit mills".

The fundamental regulatory conflict surrounding IRC § 41 stems from the divergence between the incentive's statutory design and the commercial practices of contingency-driven promoters. Originally enacted in the Economic Recovery Tax Act of 1981 (as IRC § 44F before redesignation as IRC § 30 in 1984 and IRC § 41 under the Tax Reform Act of 1986) to reward genuine technological innovation performed within the United States, the research credit requires rigorous, project-specific proof that the taxpayer confronted and systematically resolved technical uncertainty through hard-science or engineering experimentation. R&D mills bypass this evidentiary architecture by treating the credit as a mechanical payroll deduction rather than a technically gated tax incentive. Because the federal tax system operates on strict taxpayer self-assessment liability, the commercial size, marketing footprint, or perceived reputation of a third-party promoter—even including national or Big Four accounting firms—provides zero legal immunity when the IRS initiates an examination.

body.text: Operational Mechanics and Red Flags of Abusive R&D Tax Credit Mills

Abusive R&D tax credit mills exhibit a distinct cluster of financial, commercial, and operational red flags identified in IRS Dirty Dozen alerts and Audit Techniques Guides (ATGs). At the origination stage, these promoters deploy high-pressure sales campaigns—characterized by tax controversy practitioners as "slick used-car salesman" pitches—that promise "free money," guaranteed tax refunds, or the doubling and tripling of prior R&D credits before conducting any substantive evaluation of the taxpayer's books, records, or engineering workflows.
Contingent Fee Gouging and Incentive Distortion

A primary financial indicator of an R&D mill is its reliance on contingent fees directly indexed to the dollar magnitude of the calculated tax credit or refund. This compensation model creates an acute moral hazard wherein every marginal dollar of ordinary operating wage, administrative salary, or general overhead that the promoter reclassifies as a Qualified Research Expense (QRE) directly increases the promoter's immediate fee revenue, while the resulting examination liability is deferred entirely onto the taxpayer.

From a regulatory enforcement perspective, contingent fee arrangements in federal tax credit claims occupy a fiercely contested legal boundary. In 2007, the Treasury Department and the IRS amended Treasury Department Circular No. 230 (31 C.F.R. § 10.27) to prohibit practitioners from charging contingent fees for preparing or filing original tax returns, amended returns, or claims for refund or credit, specifically to prevent practitioners from exploiting the audit selection process. In Ridgely v. Lew, 55 F. Supp. 3d 89 (D.D.C. 2014), the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia enjoined the IRS from enforcing Circular 230 § 10.27's prohibition against "ordinary refund claims" prepared and filed prior to the commencement of an adversarial IRS examination, holding that pre-examination refund preparation did not constitute formal "practice" before the IRS under 31 U.S.C. § 330(a). Aggressive R&D and refund mills exploited the Ridgely gap to market contingency-based amended returns on an industrial scale. To close this regulatory gap, on December 26, 2024, the Treasury Department and the IRS issued proposed regulations (REG-116610-20, published in 2025-05 I.R.B. 638) that reclassify charging contingent fees for the preparation of original returns, amended returns, or claims for refund or credit prior to examination as "disreputable conduct" under proposed Circular 230 § 10.51, aligning federal practitioner discipline with the American Institute of Certified Public Accountants (AICPA) Code of Professional Conduct (1.000.010.14(c) and 1.510.001.01(b)) and state accountancy board prohibitions. Furthermore, the IRS Research Credit Claims Audit Techniques Guide (RCCATG) instructs examiners to inspect the outside consultant's Engagement Letter at the outset of an audit to determine whether a contingent-fee arrangement qualifies as a reportable transaction under Treas. Reg. § 1.6011-4 (such as a Confidential Transaction or a Transaction with Contractual Protection), where failure to disclose on Form 8886 exposes business taxpayers to strict-liability penalties under IRC § 6707A ranging from $10,000 to $50,000 for general reportable transactions and up to $200,000 for listed transactions.
Standardized Cut-and-Paste Substantiation and Payroll Estimation

To maintain high profit margins on contingency engagements, R&D mills minimize engineering and accounting labor by substituting standardized templates for empirical investigation. Rather than evaluating individual business components independently for each tax year as required by IRC § 41(d)(2)(A) and IRS guidance, mills utilize a non-compliant "cut-and-paste" protocol that recycles generic boilerplate descriptions across disparate projects and multi-year filing periods. In the IRS Audit Techniques Guide: Credit for Increasing Research Activities (i.e. Research Tax Credit) IRC § 41, the agency explicitly flags these consultant-generated "Prepackaged Submissions," warning examiners that generic narratives restating statutory or regulatory language fail to establish what the taxpayer actually did and how it conducted qualified research.

On the financial accounting side, mills frequently estimate QREs broadly or apply arbitrary, fixed blanket percentages—sometimes claiming 100% of wages for partially involved testers or solutions engineers, or sweeping in ineligible sales, marketing ("technical sales" or "market research"), and administrative personnel—without conducting technical interviews or compiling contemporaneous project documentation. As detailed in the IRS RCCATG, claiming QREs via "cost-center" or "hybrid" accounting methods (such as multiplying departmental W-2 wages by an estimated qualification percentage) fails to establish the mandatory statutory "nexus" linking specific employee hours and supply costs to discrete business components and qualified research activities (QRAs). Under IRC § 6001 and Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1, taxpayers bear the affirmative burden of maintaining contemporaneous books and records sufficient to substantiate claimed credits; where records are deficient, IRS examiners are authorized under Treas. Reg. § 1.6001-1(d) to issue a formal Notice of Inadequate Records via Letter 978, Letter 979, or Letter 1022. Moreover, the IRS Substantiation and Recordkeeping ATG emphasizes that the Service is not required to accept QRE estimates where actual records could be maintained, and courts refuse to permit estimation unless the taxpayer first proves that qualified research under IRC § 41(d) occurred and demonstrates that the lack of records is not an "inexactitude of their own making". Furthermore, mills routinely sweep statutorily excluded or ineligible operational activities—such as standard measurement, regulatory or building code compliance, routine quality control or inspection of materials under Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3), routine maintenance or production support, and aesthetic, style, taste, or cosmetic design under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B)—directly into the QRE base.
Ghost Preparer Practices and Extended Examination Exposure

The operational malfeasance of R&D mills frequently culminates in "ghost preparer" behavior at the point of return submission, a practice prominently highlighted in the IRS 2025 Dirty Dozen list (IR-2025-26). Under IRC § 6109(a)(4) and Treas. Reg. § 1.6109-2(d), any paid tax return preparer is statutorily required to obtain and furnish a valid Preparer Tax Identification Number (PTIN), and under IRC § 6695(b) and (c), the preparer must sign the return and include that identifying number. Failure to sign a return under IRC § 6695(b) or failure to furnish a PTIN under IRC § 6695(c) carries inflation-adjusted civil penalties of $60 per failure (capped at $31,500 per calendar year) for returns filed in 2025, rising to $65 per failure (with annual maximum caps adjusted between $32,500 and $34,500 across recent inflation adjustment periods, including Rev. Proc. 2026-35), while promoters making false or fraudulent statements regarding the tax benefits of an abusive scheme face penalties of up to 50% of the gross income derived from the activity. Fraudulent R&D promoters routinely refuse to sign the prepared tax return or omit their mandatory PTIN, making the filing appear self-prepared by the business owner. When the IRS selects the return for examination years later, the ghost preparer has already extracted its 25% to 35% upfront contingent fee and abandons the client, prompting the IRS to advise affected taxpayers to report misconduct via Form 14157 (Complaint: Tax Return Preparer), Form 14157-A (Return Preparer Fraud or Misconduct Affidavit), and Form 14242.

From a federal tax procedure perspective, while the baseline assessment statute of limitations under IRC § 6501(a) is three years from the date a return is filed (and the refund claim statute under IRC § 6511(a) is three years from filing or two years from payment), an IRS examination of improper R&D tax credits legally reaches back seven or more tax years through several distinct statutory and judicial mechanisms. First, under settled U.S. Tax Court jurisprudence—specifically Mennuto v. Commissioner, 56 T.C. 910 (1971), and Lone Manor Farms, Inc. v. Commissioner, 61 T.C. 436 (1974), aff'd, 510 F.2d 970 (3d Cir. 1975), as reaffirmed in IRS Chief Counsel Advice CCA 201548006—the IRS is legally empowered to examine and recompute tax credits originating in statute-barred ("closed") tax years seven or more years in the past whenever those credits are carried forward to reduce tax liability in an open audit year. For example, in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113 (2024), the IRS audited credit-utilization years 2015 through 2019 by disallowing research credits generated in 2013 through 2016 based on project records dating back to 2012. Second, under IRC § 6501(c)(1), if a return is false or fraudulent with the intent to evade tax, the statute of limitations never expires; crucially, under Allen v. Commissioner, 128 T.C. 37 (2007), the U.S. Tax Court established that the unlimited assessment window of IRC § 6501(c)(1) applies even when the fraudulent intent was solely that of the third-party return preparer rather than the taxpayer. Third, where aggressive tax positions accompany a substantial omission of gross income under IRC § 6501(e)(1), the assessment statute extends to six years, and under the base-period consistency mandate of IRC § 41(c)(5)(A), taxpayers must substantiate QREs in historical base years strictly consistently with current credit-year QREs rather than relying on recent-year extrapolations. In all such scenarios, the taxpayer bears sole legal liability for the accuracy of the tax return regardless of who prepared it or how aggressively the vendor marketed its brand.
Statutory and Judicial Architecture of Defensible IRC Section 41 Claims

Legitimate R&D tax credit specialization requires strict adherence to the statutory text of IRC § 41, Treasury Regulations (including Treas. Reg. §§ 1.41-2, 1.41-4, and 1.174-2), and federal tax jurisprudence. Unlike R&D mills that treat research credit preparation as an exercise in retrospective expense reclassification, compliant tax specialists anchor every claim in the contemporaneous satisfaction of the statutory four-part test at the individual business-component level.
The Four-Part Statutory Test Under IRC Section 41

Under IRC § 41(d)(1) and (d)(2)(A), to qualify as eligible research, an activity must satisfy four cumulative legal requirements applied separately to each discrete business component—defined under IRC § 41(d)(2)(B) as any product, process, computer software, technique, formula, or invention to be held for sale, lease, or license, or used by the taxpayer in a trade or business. The research must be directed toward a qualified (permitted) purpose of creating a new or improved business component under IRC § 41(d)(3)(A), it must satisfy the Section 174 / Section 174A test by being undertaken to eliminate specific technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), substantially all (80% or more) of the activities must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), and the research must be undertaken to discover information that is fundamentally technological in nature under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B).

cells: 1. Qualified Purpose (Permitted Purpose Test)
Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(ii) and § 41(d)(3)(A), research activities must be directed toward creating a new or improved business component relating to function, performance, reliability, or quality.
Sweeping in aesthetic, cosmetic, style, taste, or seasonal design modifications expressly excluded under IRC § 41(d)(3)(B), or routine customer adaptations excluded under § 41(d)(4).
2. Elimination of Technical Uncertainty (Section 174 / 174A Test)

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A) and Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(1), activities must be intended to discover information in the experimental or laboratory sense that eliminates specific unknowns concerning the capability, method, or appropriate design of the business component at project inception.
Treating routine commercial uncertainty, unknown building footprints, cost estimation, client equipment selection, or ordinary project management complexity as technical uncertainty.
3. Process of Experimentation (Substantially All Test)

Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C), at least 80% ("substantially all") of the research activities must constitute elements of a systematic process of experimentation—such as modeling, simulation, or systematic trial-and-error—designed to evaluate alternatives.

Claiming standardized multi-stage commercial workflows, routine design iterations, or basic engineering calculations using historical data where the technical solution was achievable through existing knowledge.
4. Technological in Nature (Discovery Test)
Under IRC § 41(d)(1)(B)(i), the process of experimentation must fundamentally rely on principles of the physical or biological sciences, engineering, or computer science.
Sweeping standard measurement, building code compliance, routine quality control (Treas. Reg. § 1.174-2(a)(3)), or non-technical sales and administrative payroll into qualified wage pools.

body.text: Heightened Judicial Scrutiny Under Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner

Recent federal tax litigation has substantially elevated the evidentiary threshold required to sustain an R&D tax credit claim under examination, exemplified by the U.S. Tax Court's decision on December 23, 2024, in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113. In that case, Phoenix Design Group (PDG)—a Tennessee C-corporation providing mechanical, electrical, plumbing, and fire protection (MEPF) engineering design services for hospitals, laboratories, and commercial buildings—engaged third-party consultant alliantgroup in 2017 to conduct a multi-year R&D credit study. Out of 409 to 419 total projects identified across 2012–2016, the consultant reduced the pool to 238 potentially qualifying projects, evaluated a sample of 24 projects in detail (deeming 20 qualified), and extrapolated those sample findings across all 238 projects to claim sole-wage R&D credits generated in 2013–2016 ($138,205 for 2013; $158,031 for 2014; $138,334 for 2015; and $128,228 for 2016) and utilized across tax years 2015 through 2019. Following an examination, the IRS disallowed $461,741 in utilized research credits across 2015–2019 ($55,504 for 2015; $47,811 for 2016; $219,177 for 2017; $68,147 for 2018; and $71,102 for 2019) and assessed $91,806 in accuracy-related penalties ($11,101 for 2015; $9,021 for 2016; $43,835 for 2017; $13,629 for 2018; and $14,220 for 2019), for a combined assessment of $553,547.

To adjudicate the dispute, the parties selected a nonbinding judgment sample of three trial projects—the Gerald Champion Military Psychiatric Unit, Baptist Memorial Health North Mississippi Oxford (BMHNMO), and the Vanderbilt University Engineering and Science Building (VUESB)—stipulating that if even one of the three projects involved qualified research, the IRS would concede accuracy-related penalties across all credit years. The Tax Court ruled in favor of the IRS on all three sample projects, sustaining both the credit disallowances and the accuracy-related penalties without separately excusing liability based on reliance on the outside consultant.

First, the documentation must explicitly define the specific, objective technical uncertainty regarding capability, method, or appropriate design that existed at the project's inception based on information available to the taxpayer. If a qualified professional could resolve the design challenge using available schematic block diagrams, historical data, standard engineering knowledge, or basic sizing calculations, no statutory uncertainty exists under IRC § 41(d)(1)(A). Furthermore, the Tax Court held that merely not knowing a new building's footprint or final owner-selected equipment (such as for a hybrid operating room) does not establish design uncertainty across an entire MEPF system. Second, the taxpayer must produce reliable, contemporaneous evidence—corroborated by consistent employee timesheets, design revisions, modeling, or test logs—demonstrating that the project team executed a systematic process of experimentation under IRC § 41(d)(1)(C) specifically to resolve that initial technical uncertainty, proving the investigative work conducted between the problem and the solution as previously emphasized in Little Sandy Coal Co. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2021-15, aff'd, 62 F.4th 287 (7th Cir. 2023), and Betz v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2023-84. While Phoenix Design Group does not impose a categorical ban on oral testimony or reasonable allocation estimates where properly supported, the court rejected PDG's oral testimony because employee time-tracking descriptions contradicted the claimed six-stage experimental process.

Crucially, Phoenix Design Group (echoing Leon Max v. Commissioner) confirms that activities solely involving standard measurement, adherence to building or regulatory codes without qualifying experimentation, basic calculations from historical data, or aesthetic design fail the statutory threshold. Moreover, when applying the "shrinking-back rule" of Treas. Reg. § 1.41-4(b)(2)—which requires applying the four-part test to the next most significant subset of elements when an overall business component fails—the Tax Court held that while a building's MEPF system could shrink back into a specific engineering discipline (mechanical, electrical, or plumbing), it cannot shrink back solely into a specific design phase or to the activities of individual employees. Because R&D mills rely on retrospective, employee-level or phase-level payroll allocations and generic project summaries rather than component-level experimental records, mill-prepared claims systematically collapse when audited under the Phoenix Design Group framework.
Administrative Guidance and IRC Section 174 Coordination

Beyond judicial precedent, the IRS has intensified administrative scrutiny through updated Audit Technique Guides (ATGs), Chief Counsel directives, and redesigned tax reporting forms governing how research credit claims must be disclosed and substantiated. Under IRS Chief Counsel Memorandum CCM 20214101F and Interim Guidance Memorandum LB&I-04-1222-0026, any taxpayer filing an amended return or claim for refund that includes an IRC § 41 research credit claim must satisfy the specificity mandate of Treas. Reg. § 301.6402-2(b)(1) prior to audit consideration by providing a written declaration signed under penalties of perjury that identifies all business components forming the factual basis of the claim for that tax year, describes all research activities performed by business component (what the taxpayer did and how they did it), and provides the total qualified employee wage expenses, supply expenses, and contract research expenses (along with individuals performing the research and information sought to be discovered under the initial five-item mandate, subsequently modified in IRS filing guidance to focus on business components, research activities, and QRE totals). Crucially, the IRS transition period allowing taxpayers 45 days to "perfect" deficient refund claims (via Letter 6428) expired on January 9, 2024; for deficient research credit refund claims filed on or after January 10, 2024, the IRS issues Letter 6430 (No Consideration, Section 41 Claim) outright without granting an opportunity to perfect.

Concurrently, the IRS substantially redesigned Form 6765 (Credit for Increasing Research Activities) for the 2024, 2025, and 2026 tax years by adding Section E (mandatory starting in tax year 2024) and Section G (Business Component Information), while moving the category breakout of QREs (wages, supplies, computer rental/lease costs, and contract research) to Section F. Section G requires taxpayers to report detailed qualitative and financial data—including controlled group member EIN and principal business activity code, business component classification (product, process, software, technique, formula, or invention), and wage QRE breakouts across Lines 50–53—for each business component comprising the top 80% of total QREs, up to a maximum of 50 business components. While Section G remained optional for tax years beginning in 2024 and 2025 (including under the December 2025 Form 6765 Instructions), it becomes mandatory for tax years beginning on or after January 1, 2026, for all claimants unless the taxpayer is a Qualified Small Business (QSB) opting for the payroll tax credit or has total QREs equal to or less than $1.5 million determined at the controlled group level.

Furthermore, legitimate R&D advisory practice requires navigating the complex statutory interplay between IRC § 41, IRC § 174, new IRC § 174A, and IRC § 280C(c). For tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, through December 31, 2024, the Tax Cuts and Jobs Act (TCJA) eliminated immediate expensing under IRC § 174 and mandated that taxpayers capitalize and amortize specified R&E expenditures (including software development costs) ratably over five years for domestic research and 15 years for foreign research. Following the enactment of the One Big Beautiful Bill Act (OBBBA) in 2025, Congress established new IRC § 174A, which restores immediate current-year deductibility for domestic R&E expenditures for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 (while leaving foreign R&E expenditures subject to mandatory 15-year capitalization and amortization under IRC § 174), and provides transition elections allowing general taxpayers to recover unamortized 2022–2024 domestic R&E costs immediately in 2025 or ratably over two years, and eligible small businesses (average annual gross receipts of $31 million or less for 2022–2024) to elect retroactive expensing back to tax years beginning after December 31, 2021, via amended returns. Critically, OBBBA also amended the first prong of the research credit test in IRC § 41(d)(1)(A)—requiring that qualified research expenditures "are treated" as domestic R&E expenditures under IRC § 174A rather than merely "may be treated" under § 174—and restored the applicability of IRC § 280C(c) for tax years beginning after December 31, 2024 (as well as retroactively for small businesses amending 2022–2024 returns), requiring claimants to either reduce their domestic R&E deduction by the research credit claimed or elect a reduced credit that lowers the claimed R&D credit by 21%. Volume-based R&D mills routinely ignore this mandatory accounting-method and Section 280C(c) coordination across IRC §§ 41, 174, and 174A, leaving claimants exposed to severe examination adjustments and disallowed amended claims.
Differentiating High-Compliance Specialization
Professional Authority and Multi-Disciplinary Six-Eye Review

A primary differentiator of a legitimate R&D tax specialist is verifiable regulatory standing within the tax profession. Functioning as an accredited educator providing daily free CPE/CE webinars for licensed CPAs, Certified Financial Planners (CFPs), and Enrolled Agents establishes a baseline of technical accountability that uncredentialed sales promoters cannot replicate.

Under this protocol, each claim package is independently evaluated by three separate domain professionals: a Qualified Engineer, a Scientist, and a Certified Public Accountant (CPA) or Enrolled Agent (with audit defense engagements managed by a multidisciplinary team of tax attorneys, CPAs, and engineers). This multi-disciplinary separation of duties directly addresses the evidentiary vulnerabilities exposed in Phoenix Design Group, Inc. v. Commissioner, T.C. Memo. 2024-113. Specifically, the Qualified Engineer and Scientist evaluate the project narratives and contemporaneous engineering records to verify that objective technical uncertainty existed at inception and was resolved through a systematic process of experimentation at the valid business-component or subsystem level, stripping out non-qualified routine design, building code compliance, basic calculations, or aesthetic work. Concurrently, the CPA or Enrolled Agent verifies the financial substantiation and nexus of the QREs (wages, supplies, and contract research under the 65%/75% rules of IRC § 41(b)(3)) to ensure full alignment with IRC §§ 41, 174, 174A, and Form 6765 Section G reporting standards.
Audited Quality Management Systems and AI Risk Controls

In contrast to the informal, volume-driven workflows of R&D mills, high-compliance specialization incorporates externally reviewed risk and security frameworks. From a technical standards perspective, while ISO/IEC 27001 (including its 2022 revision, ISO/IEC 27001:2022) is a formal, third-party certifiable management system standard that protects sensitive client intellectual property and financial records, ISO 31000:2009 (subsequently revised by the International Organization for Standardization as ISO 31000:2018) was published as a risk management principles-and-guidelines framework rather than a third-party certifiable management system standard; accordingly, references to ISO 31000:2009 certification in the firm's literature reflect independently reviewed adherence and alignment with ISO 31000 risk management guidelines alongside formal ISO/IEC 27001:2022 certification.

This systematic risk management architecture extends to pre-filing validation and post-filing examination support through the firm's creditARMOR platform. First, the firm explicitly discloses that AI tools (including TaxTrex and creditARMOR) can make mistakes or overlook relevant facts, mandating that all AI outputs be evaluated by a qualified tax professional via the Six-Eye Review before being relied upon or submitted to a tax authority. Even with these standard professional scope boundaries, pre-filing stress-testing and structured IDR defense stand in sharp contrast to R&D mills that extract upfront percentage fees and vanish upon receipt of an IRS examination notice.

Consider a hypothetical mid-sized engineering firm evaluating two competing R&D tax credit providers across a three-year filing window in which potential credit claims are assessed.

Under Scenario A, representing a hypothetical Dirty Dozen R&D mill, the promoter guarantees a specific refund amount during initial sales calls (red flag 1 = 1) and calculates claims using broad payroll estimates without reviewing project documentation (red flag 2 = 1), while performing zero engineer interviews (safeguard 1 = 0), offering no contractual audit defense (safeguard 2 = 0), and utilizing no separate technical and financial review teams (safeguard 3 = 0). Applying the scoring formula yields the following result:
Score<sub>Mill</sub> = Clamp<sub>0</sub><sup>100</sup> (50 + 20(0) − 25(2)) = Clamp<sub>0</sub><sup>100</sup>(50 − 50) = 0 (High Risk Tier)

Under Scenario B, representing a hypothetical high-compliance specialist, the provider conducts technical interviews with engineers and developers (safeguard 1 = 1), provides explicit audit defense support in the contract (safeguard 2 = 1), and executes a separate technical and financial Six-Eye Review (safeguard 3 = 1), with zero sales guarantees (red flag 1 = 0) and zero unsubstantiated estimates (red flag 2 = 0). Computing the specialist score yields:
Score<sub>Specialist</sub> = Clamp<sub>0</sub><sup>100</sup> (50 + 20(3) − 25(0)) = Clamp<sub>0</sub><sup>100</sup>(50 + 60) = 100 (Low Risk Tier)

To evaluate the financial consequences of these two profiles, assume the hypothetical R&D mill inflates annual QREs by sweeping in routine building code compliance, basic sizing calculations, and standard design iterations, claiming an improper research credit of $150,000 per year across 3 consecutive tax years for a total improper credit claimed of $450,000 ($150,000 × 3 years = $450,000). At the 25% contingent fee lower bound, the upfront fee is computed as $450,000 × 0.25 = $112,500, and at the 35% contingent fee upper bound, the upfront fee reaches $450,000 × 0.35 = $157,500.

When the IRS initiates an examination and disallows 100% of the unsubstantiated $450,000 credit under the Phoenix Design Group standard for failing to demonstrate inception technical uncertainty and contemporaneous experimentation, the taxpayer must repay the full $450,000 tax credit plus a 20% statutory accuracy-related penalty equal to $90,000 ($450,000 × 0.20 = $90,000), bringing the direct tax and penalty assessment to $540,000 before statutory interest. Because the ghost-preparer mill structured its contract for immediate payment and abandoned the taxpayer upon audit, the taxpayer suffers an unrecovered out-of-pocket promoter fee loss of $112,500 to $157,500 on top of the $90,000 accuracy-related penalty and unindemnified legal defense fees across an examination that can look back seven years or more via credit carryforward adjustments (Mennuto v. Commissioner) or preparer fraud exceptions (IRC § 6501(c)(1)). Conversely, under the high-compliance specialist model, non-qualifying code compliance and routine design expenses are excluded prior to filing via the Six-Eye Review and creditARMOR AI risk evaluation, fees are billed transparently on a fixed or hourly basis ($195–$395/hr), and examination defense representation on legitimate claimed credits is provided under the firm's audit defense framework.
